## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is no evidence yet beyond the starting architecture, which scored 0.000 on both seeds. Two things probably cause that. (1) The default recipe gives only 32 PPO updates (131k steps ÷ 4096 per update), which is very few. (2) The 2D trunk mixes all layers in its first 1x1 conv, so to judge a placement it must work out the landing layer (the highest build cell under the footprint) and then check the target at that layer, all inside channel mixing. That is a hard function to learn. This round is a partial factorial test. A tests a per-layer footprint scorer with a recipe that gives more updates. B keeps the baseline network and uses the same recipe, which separates the recipe effect from the architecture effect. C adds within-layer spatial context to A's network. With the budget this small, any repeatable success clearly above 0 matters.

### Round 2
All four trials so far, including the starting architecture, score 0.000 on dev and on training. That tells us nothing about which architecture is better. Two layerwise scorers (r1c1, r1c3) also scored 0. They assume a fixed channel order, which is risky if this world differs from its description. So the likely bottleneck is too few samples or updates, plus a head that has trouble linking the brick's landing layer with the target cells at that layer. With ppo_epochs=1, the budget gives about 3.25× as many env steps as the default, around 400k at r≈1, spread over about 400 small updates. This round: (A) the starting architecture with a 1-epoch, high-update recipe, to see if samples alone help. (B) A generic relational footprint head: it pools a landing-height feature over the footprint, combines it with each covered cell's full-column features, then takes min and mean over those cells. Same recipe as A. (C) B with 2 PPO epochs, to measure reusing data against collecting fresh samples.

### Round 3
All 6 trials scored exactly 0 on dev, and training success was also 0 in every run. That covers the baseline, layer-wise scorers and relational heads, and recipes with 1, 2 or 4 epochs and 32 to 416 updates. Recipe changes and footprint-aware heads made no measurable difference. Since nothing moved at all, the likeliest cause is a mismatch between this world and the stated rules, not seed noise or tuning. The task warns the world may differ from its description. Every head so far assumes that action index a lines up with obs cell (y, x) with a top-left anchor. A swapped y/x, a different anchor convention or a remapped index would break all of them, and conv layers cannot learn a transposition. This round tests heads that assume no alignment. Each maps flattened features to all logits with a learned dense layer, so any action layout can be learned.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev and on training success. They differed widely in heads (per-layer, relational, pooled, flat MLP, dense), recipes (1, 2 or 4 epochs, 64 or 256 envs, up to 426k samples) and sizes. Seed noise cannot explain a flat zero this consistent. So a factor shared by all of them is the bottleneck. Two explanations fit. First, the dense reward rewards filling target cells even when a placement seals missing cells below it. The agent then learns greedy filling and never reaches the rare +1 for an exact build, which gamma 0.95 discounts further. Second, the world may differ from its description, for example a different anchor convention, swapped brick orientations or a transposed index. Then every head that assumes top-left anchoring is misaligned, and the flat heads may just learn too slowly. This last round tests both: a head that does not assume alignment and also sees the mask, the same head plus a dense path, and a baseline with a longer horizon.
